items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The work done (energy transferred) per unit charge moving between two points, V = W/q, measured in volts"?
items.answer: potential difference
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of potential difference.

items.stem: "Electrons move through a wire at nearly the speed of light." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Electrons drift at around 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; the electric field (signal) propagates at nearly the speed of light.
items.markingKey: Electrons drift at around 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; the electric field (signal) propagates at nearly the speed of light. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A wire narrows to half its diameter in one section. In the narrow section, compared with the wide section, the current is
items.answer: the same
items.markingKey: B. Charge is conserved.

items.stem: A wire made of copper, of diameter 2 mm, carries 3.0 A. The free-electron density is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the drift speed of the electrons.
Calculate the energy transferred when 5.0 C of charge moves through a potential difference of 6.0 V.

A copper wire of diameter 1.0 mm carries a current of 3.0 A. Copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. (a) Calculate the cross-sectional area. (b) Calculate the drift speed. (c) Calculate the time for an electron to drift 1.0 m. (d) Explain why the lamp at the end of a 1.0 m wire lights immediately.
items.answer: (a) A = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m²; (b) v = I/(nAe) = 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; (c) ≈ 3.6 × 10³ s (about an hour); (d) the electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, so electrons everywhere start moving at once.
items.markingKey: (a) A = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m²; (b) v = I/(nAe) = 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹; (c) ≈ 3.6 × 10³ s (about an hour); (d) the electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, so electrons everywhere start moving at once.

items.stem: A current of 2.0 A flows for 30 s. The charge passing a point is
items.markingKey: D. Q = It.

items.stem: Explain why a lamp lights almost instantly when switched on even though electrons drift very slowly.
items.answer: The wire is already full of free electrons; the electric field is established along the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so all electrons start drifting at once.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The wire is already full of free electrons; the electric field is established along the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so all electrons start drifting at once. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A motor in a toy factory in Lima transfers 4800 J of energy in 120 s from a 6 V supply. Calculate the current in the motor.
A motor in a toy factory in Vienna transfers 1440 J of energy in 240 s from a 12 V supply. Calculate the current in the motor.

This question is about electric current, charge and potential difference.

(a) A current of 4.0 A flows through a heater element for 60 s. Calculate the charge that passes through it. [2]

(b) Distinguish between potential difference and electromotive force. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Using conventional current instead of electron flow causes confusion and should be abandoned." [6]
items.answer: (a) 240 C (b) EMF is the energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by a source (e.g. chemical → electrical); potential difference is the energy transferred from each coulomb to other forms as it passes through a component. (c) The convention is arbitrary but consistent and works for all carrier types, so it is retained (NOS: conventions).
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Q = It (M1) = 240 C (A1). (b) [4 marks] EMF is the energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by a source (e.g. chemical → electrical); potential difference is the energy transferred from each coulomb to other forms as it passes through a component. (c) [6 marks] For: electrons actually move the opposite way in metals; beginners find the convention confusing. Against: all circuit laws and symbols use the conventional direction consistently; in electrolytes and semiconductors positive carriers also move; changing would disrupt engineering practice. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: The convention is arbitrary but consistent and works for all carrier types, so it is retained (NOS: conventions).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "light-dependent resistor (LDR)"?
options: A component whose resistance decreases as the intensity of light falling on it increases
A circuit in which components are connected end to end so that the same current flows through each
A semiconductor component whose resistance decreases as its temperature increases
A series arrangement of resistors that splits the supply pd in proportion to their resistances
items.answer: A component whose resistance decreases as the intensity of light falling on it increases
items.markingKey: A. "light-dependent resistor (LDR)" is a component whose resistance decreases as the intensity of light falling on it increases.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of electrons and ions, why the resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature.
items.answer: Lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude at higher temperature, so free electrons collide with them more often; their drift is impeded more, increasing resistance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude at higher temperature, so free electrons collide with them more often; their drift is impeded more, increasing resistance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between resistivity and resistance.
items.answer: Resistance (Ω) is a property of a particular component, depending on its dimensions and temperature; resistivity (Ω m) is a property of the material, independent of the component’s size and shape.
items.markingKey: Resistance (Ω) is a property of a particular component, depending on its dimensions and temperature; resistivity (Ω m) is a property of the material, independent of the component’s size and shape. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "All conductors obey Ohm’s law." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Only ohmic conductors at constant temperature do; filament lamps, diodes and thermistors do not.
items.markingKey: Only ohmic conductors at constant temperature do; filament lamps, diodes and thermistors do not. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A wire is replaced by one of the same material that is 2 times as long and has 3 times the diameter. By what factor does the resistance change?
items.markingKey: A. R ∝ L/d² (M1); factor = 2/3² = 0.222 (A1).

items.stem:
The resistance R of different lengths L of constantan wire of diameter 0.315 mm is measured with an ohmmeter. Theory: R = ρL/A (plus a small constant contact resistance).

L / m | R / Ω
0.200 | 1.38
0.400 | 2.61
0.600 | 3.87
0.800 | 5.21
1.000 | 6.45
1.200 | 7.70

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the resistivity ρ of constantan. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State ρ with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) R (y) against L (x); (b) gradient ≈ 6.35 Ω m⁻¹; (c) 4.95 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; (d) 4.95 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ± 1 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m
items.markingKey: (a) R (y) against L (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 6.35 Ω m⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) ρ = gradient × A = 4.95 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 1 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A student investigates a 1.00 m length of constantan wire of diameter 0.315 mm. She measures V = 2.40 V when I = 0.385 A. (a) Calculate the resistance. (b) Calculate the cross-sectional area and the resistivity. (c) The micrometer reading has an uncertainty of ±0.005 mm; calculate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (d) Suggest why the wire should not carry a large current for long.
items.answer: (a) 6.23 Ω; (b) A = 7.79 × 10⁻⁸ m², ρ = 4.86 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; (c) 1.6 % in d → 3.2 % in A; (d) heating would raise the temperature and change the resistance.
items.markingKey: (a) 6.23 Ω; (b) A = 7.79 × 10⁻⁸ m², ρ = 4.86 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m; (c) 1.6 % in d → 3.2 % in A; (d) heating would raise the temperature and change the resistance.

items.stem:
This question is about resistance, resistivity and Ohm's law; I-V characteristics.

(a) A wire is replaced by one of the same material that is 0.5 times as long and has 3 times the diameter. By what factor does the resistance change? [2]

(b) Explain why a filament lamp does not obey Ohm’s law. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Ohm’s law is a fundamental law of physics." [4]
items.answer: (a) 0.0556 (b) As current increases, the filament heats up and its resistance rises, so V/I is not constant and the I–V graph curves. (c) Ohm’s law is a useful empirical rule for certain materials, not a universal law like conservation of charge.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] R ∝ L/d² (M1); factor = 0.5/3² = 0.0556 (A1). (b) [3 marks] As current increases, the filament heats up and its resistance rises, so V/I is not constant and the I–V graph curves. (c) [4 marks] For: it describes many metals accurately over wide ranges; it underpins circuit analysis. Against: it is an empirical relationship valid only under constant conditions; many components (diodes, lamps, semiconductors) do not obey it; R = V/I is a definition, not a law. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Ohm’s law is a useful empirical rule for certain materials, not a universal law like conservation of charge.

items.stem: Define the term "Ohm’s law".
items.answer: The current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions are constant
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions are constant. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: On an I–V graph for a filament lamp, the resistance at a point is found from
items.answer: V/I at that point
items.markingKey: C. R = V/I.

items.stem: Lukas writes four statements while revising resistance, resistivity and Ohm's law; I-V characteristics. Which one is a misconception?
options: Power depends on both V and I (P = VI); a high-voltage device with a small current can have low power.
Charge is conserved: the current into a component equals the current out. Energy, not current, is transferred.
R = V/I at a point; for a non-ohmic component this is not the same as the gradient. For an I–V graph, the gradient of a straight line through the origin is 1/R.
items.answer: All conductors obey Ohm’s law.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Only ohmic conductors at constant temperature do; filament lamps, diodes and thermistors do not.

items.stem: A component has a potential difference of 1.5 V across it and a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate its resistance.
Amara writes: "A thicker wire of the same material has a higher resistivity." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature; a thicker wire has lower resistance.
items.markingKey: Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature; a thicker wire has lower resistance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Ohm’s law is a fundamental law of physics." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Ohm’s law is a useful empirical rule for certain materials, not a universal law like conservation of charge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it describes many metals accurately over wide ranges; it underpins circuit analysis. Arguments against: it is an empirical relationship valid only under constant conditions; many components (diodes, lamps, semiconductors) do not obey it; R = V/I is a definition, not a law. Supported judgement: Ohm’s law is a useful empirical rule for certain materials, not a universal law like conservation of charge. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

"A voltmeter should be connected in series to measure the voltage of a component." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A voltmeter measures pd between two points, so it is connected in parallel across the component.
items.markingKey: A voltmeter measures pd between two points, so it is connected in parallel across the component. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

options: lower than the true pd without the meter
items.answer: lower than the true pd without the meter
items.markingKey: D. The meter draws current, lowering the effective resistance.

items.stem: In a circuit, a 9.0 V supply drives current through 2 Ω in series with 10 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel. Calculate the current in the 10 Ω resistor.
items.markingKey: I_total = 1.21 A (M1); pd across parallel = 6.59 V (M1); I = 0.659 A (A1).

items.markingKey: C. I_total = 1.04 A (M1); pd across parallel = 7.83 V (M1); I = 0.652 A (A1).

items.markingKey: B. R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 15.0 Ω (A1).

items.stem: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of 6.0 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. (a) Calculate the total resistance. (b) Calculate the current from the battery. (c) Calculate the pd across the parallel combination and the current in each branch. (d) Verify Kirchhoff’s laws for the circuit.

items.answer: (c) I₁ = 1.22 A, I₂ = −0.188 A, I₃ = 1.03 A; (d) charged – current flows into its positive terminal; (e) 4.25 W

items.stem: Explain why household appliances are connected in parallel rather than in series.
items.answer: Each appliance gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently; if one fails the others keep working, and total current is shared.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each appliance gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently; if one fails the others keep working, and total current is shared. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A teacher in Oslo asks a class to choose the one correct statement about series and parallel circuits and Kirchhoff's laws. Which statement should be chosen?
options: The emf of a cell is the same as its terminal pd in all circumstances.
In series the same current flows everywhere; the pd, not the current, is shared.
A thicker wire of the same material has a higher resistivity.
A kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.
items.answer: In series the same current flows everywhere; the pd, not the current, is shared.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. In series the same current flows everywhere; the pd, not the current, is shared.

items.stem: Distinguish between resistors in series and resistors in parallel.
items.answer: In series the same current flows through each and the pds add (R = R₁ + R₂); in parallel the pd is the same and the currents add (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂).
items.markingKey: In series the same current flows through each and the pds add (R = R₁ + R₂); in parallel the pd is the same and the currents add (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.markingKey: R_parallel = 4.29 Ω (M1); R_total = 7.29 Ω (M1); I = 0.824 A (A1).

items.stem: "Kirchhoff’s laws apply to all electrical circuits." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They apply very widely as statements of conservation laws, but need modification for high-frequency circuits with significant induction and radiation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they follow from conservation of charge and energy; valid for DC and low-frequency AC circuits. Arguments against: at high frequencies, changing magnetic fields mean the loop rule must include induced emfs; charge can build up in capacitors temporarily. Supported judgement: They apply very widely as statements of conservation laws, but need modification for high-frequency circuits with significant induction and radiation. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Explain why a 100 W lamp has a smaller resistance than a 40 W lamp designed for the same voltage.
items.answer: P = V²/R at fixed V, so a higher power rating requires a lower resistance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: P = V²/R at fixed V, so a higher power rating requires a lower resistance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The power dissipated in a resistor always increases with its resistance." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: With fixed current P = I²R increases with R, but with fixed voltage P = V²/R decreases as R increases.
items.markingKey: With fixed current P = I²R increases with R, but with fixed voltage P = V²/R decreases as R increases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: 270 kWh

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Smart meters will significantly reduce household electricity consumption."
items.answer: Smart meters help, mainly by enabling flexible tariffs and grid management, but on their own produce only modest reductions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real-time feedback makes users aware of waste; enables time-of-use tariffs that shift demand. Arguments against: studies show savings of only a few per cent; privacy and cost concerns; behaviour change fades over time. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "power rating".
items.answer: The power an appliance transfers when operated at its stated voltage

items.stem: Distinguish between energy and power.
items.answer: Power is the rate of energy transfer (W = J s⁻¹); energy is the total transferred (J or kWh). A high-power appliance used briefly may transfer less energy than a low-power one left on for a long time.
items.markingKey: Power is the rate of energy transfer (W = J s⁻¹); energy is the total transferred (J or kWh). items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how a potential divider with a thermistor can be used as a temperature sensor.
items.answer: As temperature rises the thermistor’s resistance falls, so its share of the supply pd falls and the pd across the fixed resistor rises; this output pd can trigger a switch. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem:
This question is about electromotive force and internal resistance; potential dividers.

(a) A battery has emf 12 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω. Calculate the maximum power it can deliver to an external resistor. [3]

(b) Distinguish between emf and terminal potential difference. [4]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "The internal resistance of a battery is a design flaw that manufacturers should eliminate." [4]
items.answer: (a) 36.0 W (b) EMF is the energy per unit charge supplied by the source; terminal pd is the energy per unit charge delivered to the external circuit, which is less than the emf by the lost volts Ir. (c) Internal resistance can be reduced but not eliminated; it is a trade-off, and sometimes a safety feature.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Maximum when R = r (M1); P = ε²/(4r) = 36.0 W (A1). items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ideal ammeter"?
options: An ammeter with zero resistance, connected in series
The work done per unit charge by a source in moving charge around a complete circuit, ε, in volts
The direction in which positive charge would flow, from + to − outside the source
A resistor with a sliding contact used to give a continuously variable output pd
items.answer: An ammeter with zero resistance, connected in series
items.markingKey: A. "ideal ammeter" is an ammeter with zero resistance, connected in series.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "coulomb"?
options: The resistance r of a source itself, which causes energy dissipation inside the source and a drop in terminal pd when current flows
The charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s
The ratio of the potential difference across a component to the current through it, R = V/I, in ohms
The work done per unit charge by a source in moving charge around a complete circuit, ε, in volts
items.answer: The charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s
items.markingKey: B. "coulomb" is the charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about electrical power and energy is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Mohammed.)
options: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of power.

items.stem: "Using conventional current instead of electron flow causes confusion and should be abandoned." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The convention is arbitrary but consistent and works for all carrier types, so it is retained (NOS: conventions).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: electrons actually move the opposite way in metals; beginners find the convention confusing. Arguments against: all circuit laws and symbols use the conventional direction consistently; in electrolytes and semiconductors positive carriers also move; changing would disrupt engineering practice. items.stem: Distinguish between resistivity and resistance.
items.answer: Resistance (Ω) is a property of a particular component, depending on its dimensions and temperature; resistivity (Ω m) is a property of the material, independent of the component’s size and shape.

items.stem: Explain why the total resistance of resistors in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistance.
items.answer: Each extra branch provides an additional path for current at the same pd, so the total current increases for the same voltage, i.e. the total resistance falls.

items.stem:
This question is about series and parallel circuits and Kirchhoff's laws.

(a) Resistors of 12 Ω, 3 Ω and 20 Ω are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance. [1]

(b) Explain the difference between resistors in parallel and resistors in series. [4]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Kirchhoff’s laws apply to all electrical circuits." [4]
items.answer: (a) 35.0 Ω (b) In series the same current flows through each and the pds add (R = R₁ + R₂); in parallel the pd is the same and the currents add (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂). (c) They apply very widely as statements of conservation laws, but need modification for high-frequency circuits with significant induction and radiation.
items.markingKey: (a) [1 marks] R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 35.0 Ω (A1). (b) [4 marks] In series the same current flows through each and the pds add (R = R₁ + R₂); in parallel the pd is the same and the currents add (1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂). (c) [4 marks] For: they follow from conservation of charge and energy; valid for DC and low-frequency AC circuits. Against: at high frequencies, changing magnetic fields mean the loop rule must include induced emfs; charge can build up in capacitors temporarily. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: They apply very widely as statements of conservation laws, but need modification for high-frequency circuits with significant induction and radiation.

items.stem: "Smart meters will significantly reduce household electricity consumption." Discuss.
items.answer: Smart meters help, mainly by enabling flexible tariffs and grid management, but on their own produce only modest reductions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real-time feedback makes users aware of waste; enables time-of-use tariffs that shift demand. Arguments against: studies show savings of only a few per cent; privacy and cost concerns; behaviour change fades over time. Supported judgement: Smart meters help, mainly by enabling flexible tariffs and grid management, but on their own produce only modest reductions. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "The internal resistance of a battery is a design flaw that manufacturers should eliminate." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Internal resistance can be reduced but not eliminated; it is a trade-off, and sometimes a safety feature.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it wastes energy as heat and reduces terminal pd. Arguments against: it is intrinsic to the electrochemistry and cannot be zero; a small internal resistance limits short-circuit currents (safety); battery design balances energy density, cost and r. Supported judgement: Internal resistance can be reduced but not eliminated; it is a trade-off, and sometimes a safety feature. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
